title: Hashing
body:
Searching is the problem; hashing is the refusal to search. Instead of comparing a key
against the things already stored, you *compute* where it must live: a [[Hash Function]]
turns the key into a table index, and you go straight there. Lookup, insert, and delete all
become $O(1)$ on average, which is the best any structure in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]
manages.

The catch is that a hash function maps a huge key space onto a small table, so two keys will
eventually land on the same index. That is a **collision**, and everything interesting about
hashing is how you handle it.

```
keys                 h(k) = k mod 7        table
----                 --------------        -----
  15  ------------->      1        0 |
  22  ------------->      1        1 | 15, 22   <- collision
   3  ------------->      3        2 |
                                   3 | 3
```

## Collision resolution

**Separate chaining.** Each slot holds a [[Linked List]] of every key that hashed there.
Insert prepends to the list; lookup hashes, then scans that one list. Simple, degrades
gracefully, and the table can hold more entries than it has slots. The cost is a pointer
chase per probe and the memory for the nodes.

**Open addressing.** Everything lives in the table itself, and a collision sends you
looking for another slot by *probing*.

| Scheme | Next slot tried | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Linear probing | $h(k) + 1, +2, +3, \dots$ | primary clustering: occupied runs grow and merge |
| Quadratic probing | $h(k) + 1, +4, +9, \dots$ | secondary clustering; may not visit every slot |
| Double hashing | $h(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)$ | needs a second hash function, but spreads best |

Open addressing makes deletion awkward: blanking a slot breaks the probe chain of anything
that collided past it, so deleted slots are marked with a tombstone rather than emptied.

## Load factor

$$\alpha = \frac{\text{entries}}{\text{slots}}$$

This is the dial that controls performance. Chaining stays usable past $\alpha = 1$ (the
average chain is just $\alpha$ long); open addressing degrades sharply as $\alpha$
approaches 1, because the probes get longer and longer, and it is normally kept below about
0.7. Past the threshold the table **rehashes**: allocate a bigger table, usually about
double, and reinsert every key, since the indices depend on the table size. That single
resize is $O(n)$, and it is amortised over all the cheap inserts the same way a
[[Dynamic Arrays|dynamic array]] amortises its growth.

## Cost

| Operation | Average | Worst |
|---|---|---|
| Search | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Insert | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Delete | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |

The worst case is every key colliding, at which point the table is one long list and you
have a linear scan. It needs a genuinely bad hash function (or adversarial input) to happen,
but it is a real bound, and it is why a [[Balanced Tree]] with its guaranteed $O(\log n)$ is
sometimes preferred over an average-case $O(1)$.

What hashing does *not* give you is order. There is no "next key", no range query, and no
sorted traversal, because the hash function deliberately scatters keys. That is the whole
trade against a [[Binary Search Tree]].

## How soon do collisions start

Sooner than intuition says, and the answer is a [[Probability]] calculation rather than a data
structures one. It is the **birthday problem**: 23 people give a better-than-even chance of a
shared birthday out of 365, because what grows is the number of *pairs*, $\binom{n}{2}$, not $n$.
Applied to a table, collisions become likely at around $\sqrt{m}$ keys for $m$ buckets, so a
million-bucket table starts colliding at about a thousand keys.

**That is why collision resolution is a required feature and not a rare-case fallback.** The
average number of keys per bucket under a good hash function follows a Poisson distribution with
$\lambda = n/m$ (see [[Probability Distribution]]), and the expected $O(1)$ lookup claim above is
an expectation over that distribution rather than a guarantee. [[STATISTICS]] owns
both arguments.

## Not the cryptographic kind

Same word, almost opposite design brief, and the confusion is worth heading off. A
[[Cryptographic Hash Function]] is built so that you **cannot** invert it and
**cannot** find two inputs that agree; this one is built to be fast and to spread keys evenly, and
it may be trivially invertible without anybody minding.

| | Hashing (here) | [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] |
|---|---|---|
| Wants | speed, uniform spread over $m$ buckets | pre-image and collision resistance |
| Collisions | **expected**, handled below | a **break** of the function |
| Output | table-sized, $h(k) = k \bmod m$ | fixed and large, 256+ bits |
| Invertible | irrelevant | must not be |
| Adversary | none, keys are just data | assumed and funded |

`k mod 7` is fine here and useless there. SHA-256 is fine there and absurd here, thousands of times
slower than a problem with no adversary needs. The one thing they genuinely share is the birthday
argument below: it is why this note needs collision resolution at all, and why a digest has to be
twice as long as the security level it claims.

## The algebra under `mod`

$h(k) = k \bmod m$ is [[Modular Arithmetic]], and a bucket **is** a congruence class: two keys
collide exactly when $k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod m$. That reading also explains the standard advice to
pick $m$ prime. $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a [[Field]] and $\mathbb{Z}_m$ for composite $m$ is not, so with
a composite table size any key sharing a factor with $m$ lands in a restricted set of buckets, and
patterned keys pile up. [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] owns that argument.
